lesson.title: Reversing the Secant Rule: The Integral of sec(x)tan(x)
lesson.summary: The product sec(x)*tan(x) looks intimidating until you recognize it as exactly the derivative of sec(x), which makes its integral simply sec(x).
lesson.body:
The integral of sec(x)*tan(x) is: integral of sec(x)*tan(x) dx = sec(x) + C.

This rule comes from the derivative of secant: the derivative of sec(x) is sec(x)*tan(x). Since differentiating sec(x) produces exactly the product sec(x)*tan(x), sec(x) is, by definition, an antiderivative of sec(x)*tan(x). As with every rule in this unit, the integral fact is simply the derivative fact read from right to left.

This rule looks a little different from the four before it, because the integrand is a product of two different trig functions rather than a single function or a squared function. Recognizing that a product like sec(x)*tan(x) matches a derivative you already know, rather than trying to integrate sec(x) and tan(x) separately, is the key skill being reinforced here. Spotting this kind of match is exactly the reverse engineering approach introduced back in the basic trig integrals overview, now applied to a product instead of a single function.

Worked example: find integral of 6*sec(x)*tan(x) dx. Apply the constant multiple rule: 6 * integral of sec(x)*tan(x) dx = 6*sec(x) + C. Verify by differentiating: the derivative of 6*sec(x) is 6*sec(x)*tan(x), which matches the original integrand.

Keep the domain restriction in mind as well: sec(x) and tan(x) are both undefined at odd multiples of pi/2, so the rule applies on intervals that avoid those points, matching exactly where sec(x)*tan(x) itself is undefined.
